```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(medfate)
library(medfateland)
library(meteoland)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Introduction

The aim of this vignette is to illustrate the sensitivity of watershed ecohydrological simulations (e.g. via `spwb_land()`) to variations in three watershed parameters for sub-model TETIS. A global sensitivity analysis was carried out to identify which parameters users should focus on when calibrating MEDFATELAND and which can be fixed at default values. 

## Sensitivity analysis procedure

### Synthetic catchment

To characterise the hydrological behaviour of the model independently of a particular catchment, the analysis was performed on a synthetic catchment of 15 x 20 = 300  cells at 500 m resolution (750 ha), representing a linear valley with 5\% slope and lateral hill slopes with 25\% slope. All cells had aforest consisting of a single cohort of Pinus nigra trees of 8m height, 20 cm DBH and stand LAI = 2; and a soil taken from a cell in Aiguadora catchment. Daily weather forcing was also taken from the same catchment. Watershed hydrology simulations were run using the `spwb_land()` function and included a warm-up period (2000-2010) followed by the analysis period (2011-2020).

The following shows the `sf` object representing the synthetic catchment:

```{r, warning=FALSE}
sensitivity_path = "~/mcaceres_work/model_development/medfateland_sensitivity/data/SA_morris_results_single_DTB40000/"
ws_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(tibble::as_tibble(readRDS(file.path(sensitivity_path,"ws_sf.rds"))))
ws_sf
```

Another spatial input is needed to describe the grid topology, which in our case is an object of class `SpatRaster` from package **terra** matching the coordinate definition in the `sf` object:

```{r}
nx <- 15
ny <- 20
res <- 500
xmin <- 400000
ymin <- 4670000
crs <- "epsg:32631"
r <- terra::rast(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmin + nx * res,
                   ymin = ymin, ymax = ymin + ny * res,
                   nrows = ny, ncols = nx, crs = crs)
```

The topography of the synthetic watershed looks as follows:

```{r,  fig.align='center', fig.width=7, height = 4}
plot_variable(ws_sf, variable = "elevation", r = r)
```

### Design of parameter exploration

The analysis considered the seven effective parameters of the lateral and vertical flow formulation: $n_{\mathrm{interflow}}$, $n_{\mathrm{baseflow}}$, $R_{\mathrm{localflow}}$, $R_{\mathrm{interflow}}$, $R_{\mathrm{baseflow}}$, $D_{\mathrm{loss}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{Manning}}$. The following table provides parameter limits for exploration, as well as default values for a reference run (see below), and indicates whether sampling is performed on a logarithmic scale:

```{r}
par_def <- data.frame(
  name  = c("n_interflow", "n_baseflow", "R_localflow", "R_interflow",
            "R_baseflow", "deep_aquifer_loss", "n_manning"),
  label = c("n[interflow]", "n[baseflow]", "R[localflow]", "R[interflow]",
            "R[baseflow]", "D[loss]", "n[Manning]"),
  log10 = c(TRUE,  FALSE, TRUE,  TRUE,  TRUE,  FALSE, FALSE),
  min   = c(0.01,  0.01,   0.1,   0.1,     0.1,   0,     0.01),
  max   = c(2,     2,     20,    20,   20,    5,     0.1),
  ref   = c(0.08391252,   0.57094430,  0.87305020,     1.65763220,     
            0.21474088,   3.73822300,  0.06943110), 
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
par_def
```

As procedure for sensitivity analysis we used the elementary effects method of Morris, implemented in function `morris()` (of package **sensitivity**), which provides a robust ranking of parameter importance at a small fraction of the cost of variance-based methods. Each parameter was sampled over the range given in the previous table, discretised into six levels, and $r = 20$ trajectories were generated, giving $r(k+1) = 160$ model runs for $k = 7$ parameters:

```{r}
r_traj <- 20 # Number of trajectories
n_levels <- 6 # Number of levels for each parameter

# Limits in the sampling scale (logarithmic for some parameters)
binf <- ifelse(par_def$log10, log10(par_def$min), par_def$min)
bsup <- ifelse(par_def$log10, log10(par_def$max), par_def$max)

# Morris design
mo <- sensitivity::morris(model = NULL, factors = par_def$name, r = r_traj,
                          design = list(type = "oat", levels = n_levels,
                                        grid.jump = n_levels / 2),
                          binf = binf, bsup = bsup, scale = TRUE)
dim(mo$X)
head(mo$X)
```



### Simulations

We first run `spwb_land()` on the synthetic watershed with parameters calibrated for the Aiguadora catchment. Then, we made simulations for each of the 160 parameter combinations of the morris design. Each simulation included 11 years of warm-up simulation, followed by 10 years of simulation for analysis. Simulations were conducted using 1D Richards for local soil water flows (`soilDomains = "single"`), with a tolerance value `richards_tolerance = 0.00001`; and 24 daily substeps were specified for lateral processes, using the watershed control parameter `num_daily_substeps = 24`. For all these runs, we stored the simulated daily discharge, as well as water balance components (precipitation, transpiration, runoff...) averaged at the watershed level.


### Response variables

Three groups of response variables were analysed. First, the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) of simulated daily discharge was computed against the simulated discharge in reference simulation run, as an aggregate measure of how much each parameter modifies the hydrograph. Second, six hydrological signatures of the simulated discharge were used to identify which aspect of the hydrological response is controlled by each parameter. Third, the partitioning of precipitation into evapotranspiration, surface runoff, deep drainage and losses to the deep aquifer was analysed to assess whether hydrological parameters also affect the balance between green and blue water, and transpiration was included to evaluate their effect on vegetation functioning. 

### Morris indices

Morris indices $\mu*$ and $\sigma$ were estimated using function `sensitivity::tell()` for each response variable. $\mu*$ values were normalized by response variable to the [0-1] scale, in order to compare indices between response variables that have different units.

## Results

We read the CSV corresponding to the normalized indices:

```{r}
morris_indices <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sensitivity_path, "morris_indices.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
morris_indices
```

### KGE


```{r, out.width='90%', fig.align="center", echo=TRUE, fig.alt = "Morris sensitivity results for KGE"}
d_kge <- subset(morris_indices, output == "KGE")
ggplot(d_kge, aes(mu_star, sigma, label = label)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    geom_text(parse = TRUE, vjust = -0.8, size = 3.5) +
    labs(x = expression(mu^"*"), y = expression(sigma), title = "KGE (daily discharge)") +
    theme_bw()
```

### Heatmap

```{r, out.width='90%', fig.align="center", echo=TRUE, fig.alt = "Heat map with morris sensitivity results"}
heat_out <- c("RunoffRatio", "BFI", "Q5", "Q95", "ZeroFlowFrac", "RecessionK", "HalfFlowDate",
                "ET_P", "SurfRunoff_P", "DeepDrainage_P", "DeepAqLoss_P", "Transpiration")
d_heat <- subset(morris_indices, output %in% heat_out)
d_heat$output <- factor(d_heat$output, levels = heat_out)
d_heat$label  <- factor(d_heat$label, levels = rev(par_def$label))

ggplot(d_heat, aes(output, label, fill = mu_star_norm)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#08519c", limits = c(0, 1),
                        name = expression("Normalised " * mu^"*")) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = function(l) parse(text = l)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```
